public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.

notes.text:
# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Reaction performance depends categorically on catalyst, solvent, temperature, and residence time; the anonymous indices imply no ordering. Initial screening will hold charge and workup broadly constant while varying these factors. A useful catalyst/solvent/temperature combination should give higher HPLC conversion/yield with limited byproduct than alternatives; this would justify focused workup optimization.

## H2 [tentative]
Liquid-liquid extraction followed by retaining the organic phase should enrich the target, but extractant identity and wash severity may trade recovery against purity. If final purity remains below 0.80 despite adequate reaction yield, subsequent batches will vary extraction/wash rather than reaction conditions.

## Decision rule
Use the 12 shared nonfinal measurements chiefly as one diagnostic HPLC per batch. Recommend the completed batch with the highest observed recovery among those with final-assay purity at least 0.80, treating close noisy differences cautiously and considering mass-balance error.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only as a qualitative screen]
Reaction outcomes depend strongly on the categorical recipe. In the first diagonal screen, the C1/S1 recipe at 380 K and 3600 s had the highest pre-workup HPLC conversion, yield, selectivity, and purity among batches 1–4 (event runner-operation-0021). C0/S0 was much less converted (runner-operation-0005), while C2/S2 and C3/S3 were impurity-rich (runner-operation-0037; runner-operation-0051). Temperature/time are confounded with category, so this does not identify whether C1 or S1 is causal. Next, cross C1 or S1 with other partners under more comparable conditions.

## H2 [revised]
The target largely remains outside the retained organic cuts under the tested extractions: organic selection produced very low final recovery in batches 1–2 (runner-operation-0016; runner-operation-0032), whereas aqueous selection preserved more recovery in batches 3–4 (runner-operation-0046; runner-operation-0060) but remained impure. This supports retaining aqueous for screening, but the evidence is confounded by different reaction recipes and extractants. If a high-selectivity reaction is found, compare aqueous versus organic workups and extractants directly.

## Current decision
Prioritize reaction-selectivity mapping before aggressive workup optimization. Recommend only a batch meeting final purity >=0.80; none of the first four does.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in the tested design space]
Catalyst C1 paired with solvent S2 was the best tested reaction recipe. Under 360 K for 7200 s it gave the strongest pre-workup HPLC yield/recovery among the campaign screens (runner-operation-0107), and a repeat using the same reaction conditions showed a broadly similar high-yield reaction despite measurement/process variation (runner-operation-0153). Crossed screens show C2 and C3 were poorer with S1 (runner-operation-0065; runner-operation-0079), while C1 was poorer with S0 or S3 (runner-operation-0093; runner-operation-0121). This supports a categorical C1/S2 interaction within the explored range, not an ordering of anonymous indices.

## H2 [supported with limitations]
For the tested extractants, retaining aqueous preserves substantially more target than retaining organic. Batch 8's aqueous X3 workup achieved final recovery about 0.256 and purity about 0.619 (runner-operation-0116). The corresponding organic X3 strategy after the same reaction conditions yielded only about 0.021 recovery and 0.347 purity (runner-operation-0164). Repeated aqueous extraction did not improve purity at the lower-temperature reaction (runner-operation-0148), and repeated organic washing severely depleted target (runner-operation-0183). Thus aggressive washing/extraction is not justified here.

## Constraint finding
No completed batch reached final purity 0.80. The numerical leader under the stated recovery objective is batch 8: it has the highest observed final recovery while also having the highest final purity among the meaningful-recovery aqueous products. This is a best-available recommendation, not evidence that the purity constraint was satisfied. Batch-to-batch differences close to assay noise would require replication, but batch 8's margin over the other final recoveries is large enough to guide selection.

## Final source-stage decision
Select completed batch 8 (C1/S2, 360 K, 7200 s; quench; aqueous plus X3 extraction; retain aqueous; concentrate) as the best observed compromise. A future campaign should explore purification modes not available/tested here or gentler selective separations to raise purity above 0.80 without the target losses observed in organic cuts.

payload.report:
Mechanism report

1. Scope and evidence base

This account describes only the anonymous ChemWorld system explored in the completed 12-batch campaign. Catalyst, solvent, and extractant indices are independent categorical labels, not an ordered series or identified real chemicals. The conclusions therefore apply to the tested combinations, charges, temperatures, residence times, and phase operations; they should not be translated into claims about real compounds.

Each batch began with 0.040 mol limiting reagent, 0.040 L reaction solvent, and 0.005 mol catalyst. I used one pre-workup HPLC observation per batch and a final assay after termination. The HPLC and final assay do not necessarily measure identical material: HPLC characterized the reactor liquid before phase workup, whereas the final assay characterized the selected, processed phase. Consequently, large changes between those readings reflect both phase selection and processing, not continued reaction alone.

2. Proposed reaction model

A minimal explanation is a competitive network:

R -> P  with effective rate kP(catalyst, solvent, T)
R -> I  with effective rate kI(catalyst, solvent, T)
P -> D  with effective degradation rate kD(catalyst, solvent, T)

Here R is the limiting reactant, P the target, I non-target reaction products, and D degradation products. For a fixed recipe, a useful qualitative model is

dR/dt = -(kP + kI)R,
dP/dt = kP R - kD P.

The effective rate constants are categorical response surfaces rather than simple monotonic functions of material index. Temperature and time increase conversion, but their net value depends on whether productive formation or competing chemistry is accelerated more strongly. Apparent selectivity can therefore fall even while conversion rises.

The experiments support a strong catalyst–solvent coupling. The best tested pair was catalyst C1 with solvent S2. At 360 K for 7200 s, batch 8 gave pre-workup HPLC conversion 0.6169, yield 0.3420, selectivity 0.5188, purity 0.5705, and apparent recovery 0.3400. Batch 11 repeated the same reaction recipe before applying a different workup and gave similar HPLC conversion 0.6189, yield 0.3511, selectivity 0.4926, purity 0.5720, and recovery 0.3167. The agreement in conversion, yield, and purity is the strongest repeatability evidence in the campaign, although the selectivity/recovery differences show process or measurement variation.

Changing either member of that pair generally reduced performance. With C1 at 360 K and 7200 s, solvent S0 in batch 7 gave HPLC yield 0.2298 and purity 0.4970; S3 in batch 9 gave yield 0.1895 and purity 0.3602; S2 in batch 8 gave yield 0.3420 and purity 0.5705. With solvent S1 at 360 K and 7200 s, C2 in batch 5 gave yield 0.0813 and purity 0.1610, whereas C3 in batch 6 gave yield 0.1702 and purity 0.3625. These comparisons support interactions rather than an ordering such as “higher catalyst index is better.”

C1/S1 was also moderately productive. Batch 2, run at 380 K for 3600 s, gave HPLC conversion 0.4063, yield 0.2219, selectivity 0.5234, and purity 0.5851. Because both temperature/time and materials differed from many other batches, this result cannot isolate a temperature effect or establish whether S1 is intrinsically inferior to S2.

C0/S0 in batch 1 at 360 K for 1800 s was comparatively slow: HPLC conversion was 0.1482 and yield 0.0591, although selectivity was 0.4492. C2/S2 in batch 3 at 400 K for 3600 s produced conversion 0.5454 but only 0.1299 yield, 0.2453 selectivity, and 0.2673 purity. C3/S3 in batch 4 at 340 K for 7200 s produced conversion 0.4465, yield 0.0792, selectivity 0.1889, and purity 0.2390. These observations are consistent with substantial competitive byproduct formation in poorly matched catalyst–solvent pairs.

Batch 10 provides limited evidence about temperature for C1/S2. At 340 K for 3600 s it gave conversion 0.3132, yield 0.1504, selectivity 0.5746, and purity 0.6023. Compared with batches 8 and 11 at 360 K for 7200 s, the cooler/shorter condition had higher apparent selectivity and purity but much lower conversion and yield. Temperature and time changed together, so their individual effects are unidentifiable. The result nevertheless suggests the usual kinetic tradeoff: longer/hotter operation increases target production but also accumulates competing material, while milder operation preserves composition quality at the cost of recovery.

Batch 12 tested C0/S2 at 360 K for 7200 s and gave HPLC conversion 0.5365, yield 0.2480, selectivity 0.4541, and purity 0.4635. This was better than C0/S0 in batch 1, although residence time also differed, and worse than the replicated C1/S2 recipe. It reinforces the view that both catalyst and solvent contribute.

3. Proposed extraction and purification model

After reaction, I model the phase operation by distribution coefficients

DP = [P]organic/[P]aqueous,
DI = [I]organic/[I]aqueous.

For one equilibrium contact with phase-volume ratio q = Vorg/Vaq, the organic fraction of species j would be approximately

fj,org = Dj q/(1 + Dj q).

A useful extraction requires DP/DI to favor the selected phase. The campaign instead indicates that, under the tested conditions, much of the target remains in the aqueous phase and the tested organic cuts are not selectively enriched in it. Workup recovery is therefore the product of reaction yield and a sequence of retention factors:

final target recovery ≈ reaction target fraction × extraction retention × wash retention × concentration/handling retention.

The strongest direct phase-selection comparison is between batches 8 and 11. Both used C1/S2 at 360 K for 7200 s and extractant X3. Batch 8 retained the aqueous phase and finished at purity 0.6189 and recovery 0.2563. Batch 11 retained the organic phase, washed, dried, and concentrated it; its final purity was only 0.3468 and recovery 0.0212. The approximately twelve-fold recovery difference is much larger than the modest difference between their pre-workup HPLC readings. Thus phase selection, not reaction variation, caused most of the divergence. A plausible interpretation is DP < 1 for the target under X3 conditions, or at least that the target is much less organic-preferring than would be required for an efficient organic isolation.

Other organic selections behaved similarly. Batch 1 used X0 and finished with nominal purity 0.6941 but recovery reported as 0 and yield 0.0083. Batch 2 used X1 and finished at purity 0.5376 and recovery 0.0233. These cuts could appear moderately pure because almost all solute was removed, not because they recovered useful target quantities. The nearly zero recovery makes their purity values operationally unattractive and potentially noise-sensitive.

Aqueous selection preserved more target. Batch 3 finished at purity 0.2443 and recovery 0.1099; batch 4 at 0.2622 and 0.0816; batch 5 at 0.1602 and 0.0695; batch 6 at 0.4120 and 0.1484; batch 7 at 0.5031 and 0.1955; batch 8 at 0.6189 and 0.2563; and batch 9 at 0.3878 and 0.1608. Much of this variation originates in the different reactions, so it cannot identify extractant distribution coefficients separately. Still, the consistent contrast with the low-recovery organic products supports aqueous retention as the better tested policy.

More processing was not automatically more selective. Batch 10 applied two X3 contacts while retaining aqueous after a milder C1/S2 reaction. It ended at purity 0.5791 and recovery 0.1167, compared with its pre-workup HPLC purity 0.6023 and recovery 0.1637. Thus the extra contact caused loss without demonstrated enrichment. This comparison is not a clean test against batch 8 because reaction temperature/time also differed, but within batch 10 the direction of the before/after change gives no evidence for a beneficial second extraction.

Batch 12 subjected an X0 organic cut to four large washes. It ended at purity 0.0422 and recovery 0, despite pre-workup HPLC purity 0.4635 and recovery 0.2349. The washes therefore did not behave as selective impurity removal; they depleted or displaced the target disproportionately. Batch 11 likewise shows that washing/drying an organic phase did not rescue X3 extraction. A plausible process explanation is repeated multiplicative loss: after n operations with target-retention fraction rP, retained target scales as rP^n. Even a moderate loss per contact becomes severe after four washes.

4. Interpretation of the final assays

Final-assay “conversion” after organic isolation sometimes approached one even when pre-workup conversion was modest: batch 1 reported final conversion 0.9946 after pre-workup HPLC conversion 0.1482, and batch 2 reported 1.000 after 0.4063. These numbers should not be interpreted as reaction continuing to completion during extraction. The selected organic sample can be depleted in original reactant, causing composition-based conversion to appear high while containing almost no target. This is supported by the simultaneous low final selectivity and recovery: batch 1 final selectivity was 0.0124 with recovery 0, and batch 2 selectivity was 0.0109 with recovery 0.0233. Therefore recovery relative to original charge is the more reliable cross-stage performance metric.

Final process mass-balance errors were small in reported magnitude, generally zero to approximately 0.0065. Examples include 0.00646 in batch 8 and 0 in batches 2, 5–7, and 9–11. This argues against gross numerical imbalance as the explanation for the main recovery differences, although it cannot distinguish physical phase loss from chemically transformed target.

The observed peak safety risks were below the campaign limit of 0.65; the highest displayed pre-workup values were around 0.35. Safety therefore did not bind the tested optimization. The displayed cost saturated at 1 for most developed batches and is not sufficiently resolved to support a quantitative cost model.

5. How the explanation changed during the campaign

The first two batches initially suggested that organic extraction might improve purity: batch 1’s final purity was 0.6941 and batch 2’s was 0.5376. However, their recoveries were 0 and 0.0233. This changed the interpretation from “organic extraction purifies the target” to “organic isolation removes most material and can yield a superficially purer but target-poor cut.”

Batches 3 and 4 tested aqueous retention and preserved more target, though their reaction recipes were intrinsically impurity-rich. Batches 5–9 then separated some catalyst and solvent effects. These established C1/S2 as the best tested reaction combination and showed that aqueous X3 workup in batch 8 gave the best final recovery.

Batch 10 challenged the idea that repeated extraction must improve purity; it did not. Batch 11 provided the most informative controlled contrast in the campaign because its reaction recipe matched batch 8: switching from aqueous to organic retention collapsed recovery from 0.2563 to 0.0212. Batch 12 finally showed that repeated washing can be actively destructive rather than merely conservative.

6. Best-supported operating picture

Within the explored region, the world behaves like a coupled reaction/separation system rather than two independently optimizable stages:

1. Catalyst and solvent jointly set productive and competing reaction rates.
2. Temperature and time trade conversion against selectivity and degradation/byproduct accumulation.
3. The target is preferentially retained in the aqueous side of the tested extraction systems.
4. Organic selection and repeated washing multiply target losses.
5. Final purity cannot be inferred from apparent conversion of a selected cut; recovery relative to original charge must remain explicit.

A qualitative pseudocode representation is:

rates = reaction_surface[catalyst, solvent, temperature]
reactor = integrate_competing_reactions(initial_R, rates, time)
for contact in extraction_sequence:
    reactor = partition(reactor, extractant, aqueous_volume, organic_volume)
    reactor = retain(selected_phase)
for wash in washes:
    reactor = apply_species_specific_retention(reactor, wash)
final_metrics = assay(selected_material, denominator=initial_R)

The best observed implementation was batch 8: C1/S2, 360 K, 7200 s, followed by quench, aqueous addition, X3 contact, aqueous retention, and concentration. It achieved final recovery 0.2563 and purity 0.6189. This is the best observed compromise, not a constraint-satisfying solution: no completed batch reached the required purity of 0.80.

7. Unidentifiable factors and plausible alternatives

The catalyst and solvent main effects are not fully separable from their interaction because only a sparse subset of the 4×4 matrix was tested. Several early batches also changed temperature and time together with categorical materials. Exact kinetic constants, activation energies, equilibrium constants, and distribution coefficients cannot be estimated from one time point per recipe.

Except for the nearly repeated pre-workup C1/S2 conditions in batches 8 and 11, there were no true recipe replicates. Instrument noise is specified, but process variability and stochastic simulation effects are not independently estimated. Small differences should therefore not be overinterpreted.

The HPLC-to-final changes could combine phase partition, sample-basis changes, handling loss, continued quench chemistry, and instrument-specific definitions. The available evidence strongly identifies phase selection as important but cannot uniquely decompose those mechanisms.

An alternative reaction explanation is that solvent primarily controls analytical response or phase microenvironment rather than intrinsic kinetics. The similar batch 8/11 reaction readings make gross analytical artifacts less likely for C1/S2, but the anonymous system prevents molecular validation. Another alternative is reversible product formation with solvent-dependent equilibrium rather than irreversible competing kinetics; the available single-time observations cannot discriminate equilibrium from kinetics.

The apparent aqueous preference might be extractant-specific ionization or association rather than an intrinsic polarity of the target. Because pH, salt composition, and molecular identity were unavailable, no acid–base or complexation mechanism can be assigned. X3 may also preferentially remove certain impurities while still losing some target; batch 8’s increased final purity relative to its pre-workup value is compatible with limited impurity removal, but batch 10 shows that repeating the contact is not necessarily beneficial.

Finally, the failure to reach purity 0.80 does not establish that the threshold is impossible. It establishes only that the tested reaction/extraction/wash sequences did not reach it. Unexplored catalyst–solvent combinations, independent optimization of time and temperature, different phase ratios, staged recovery of both phases, back-extraction, or purification operations outside the tested sequence could plausibly improve purity while preserving recovery.

payload.rationale: All queries retain the organic phase, whereas the campaign’s strongest controlled comparison showed that organic retention caused severe target loss: with the same C1/S2 reaction and X3 contact, batch 8’s aqueous product had recovery 0.2563, while batch 11’s washed organic product had recovery 0.0212. Batch 7, which used X2 but retained aqueous, also implies that most target remained outside the X2 organic phase. I therefore predict low organic recovery throughout, with broad intervals because X2 organic partitioning was never directly assayed. Q01–Q06 use only 0.00025 mol catalyst with 0.040 mol reagent, one-twentieth of the campaign catalyst/reagent ratio. I expect low productive conversion, especially at 1800 s in Q01; extending to 7200 s raises Q02 recovery but may also accumulate impurities. X0 in Q03 is assigned higher purity but lower recovery than X2 in Q04, reflecting batch 1’s relatively pure yet essentially target-empty X0 organic cut. For X2, increasing organic volume from Q05 to Q06 should extract more target and more impurities, raising recovery while diluting selectivity; the smaller organic phase is predicted to be purer but less productive. Q07–Q12 restore the campaign catalyst/reagent ratio because the reagent charge falls to 0.002 mol. Dilution and 400 K remain extrapolations, but these recipes should generate more target per original charge than Q01–Q06. Q07 omits washing and consequently has the highest predicted organic recovery. Q08 includes a large wash; campaign batches 11 and 12 indicate that washing organic material can remove target rather than selectively improve it, so both recovery and expected purity are reduced. Splitting the same total wash into two contacts in Q10 is predicted to produce greater multiplicative target loss than the single wash in Q09. Concentration removes mainly solvent and should have little effect on solute-defined purity or recovery, so Q11 and Q12 are nearly identical, with a small allowance for handling loss in Q12. The 0.97 transfer factor and destructive HPLC sampling are included as small common recovery penalties. Predictive intervals are much wider than final-assay noise because the recipes extrapolate to lower catalyst loading, lower reagent concentration, 400 K, different phase ratios, and an unobserved X2-organic endpoint.

payload.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested claims

No instance prior, nominal material-property claim, or prescribed mechanistic law was supplied. The anonymous material labels carried no chemical ordering, so all substantive claims were developed from campaign evidence.

Supported:
- A catalyst–solvent interaction matters. C1/S2 at 360 K and 7200 s gave closely similar pre-workup results in batches 8 and 11: HPLC conversion 0.6169/0.6189, yield 0.3420/0.3511, and purity 0.5705/0.5720. C1 performed less well with S0 in batch 7 and S3 in batch 9, while C2 and C3 were poor with S1 in batches 5 and 6. This supports a categorical interaction, although it does not separately identify catalyst and solvent main effects.
- A milder reaction can trade conversion for selectivity. Batch 10, using C1/S2 at 340 K for 3600 s, had lower conversion and yield than batches 8 and 11 but higher HPLC selectivity and purity. Because time and temperature changed together, only the combined tradeoff is supported.
- The target was retained much better in the aqueous phase than in the tested organic cuts. The evidence that most changed my judgment was the comparison of batches 8 and 11. Their upstream C1/S2 reactions were nearly replicated, but aqueous retention in batch 8 produced final recovery 0.2563, whereas organic retention in batch 11 produced only 0.0212. Earlier organic batches 1 and 2 had already shown recoveries of 0 and 0.0233, but those recipes were more confounded.
- Repeated processing can multiply target loss. Two aqueous X3 contacts in batch 10 did not improve purity relative to its pre-workup reading, and four washes of the organic X0 cut in batch 12 ended with recovery 0 and purity 0.0422.

Contradicted or revised:
- My initial tentative expectation that ordinary liquid–liquid extraction followed by organic retention would enrich the target was contradicted. Batch 1 initially appeared encouraging on purity alone (0.6941), but its recovery was 0. Batch 2 was similarly weak, and batch 11 provided the decisive controlled contrast.
- The implicit idea that additional extraction or washing should monotonically improve purity was contradicted by batches 10 and 12. More contacts caused loss without demonstrated enrichment.
- The idea that high final-assay conversion necessarily indicates successful reaction was contradicted by batches 1 and 2: final conversion was approximately 0.995–1.000 while selectivity and recovery were near zero. Selected-phase composition can remove residual reactant and create high apparent conversion without useful target recovery.

Untested or unresolved:
- The differential-equation scheme R→P, R→I, and P→D remains a plausible organizing model, not an identified kinetic law. No time series at fixed temperature and composition was collected, so rate constants, reaction orders, reversibility, and activation energies remain unknown.
- Exact distribution coefficients for target and impurities were not measured. The phase results support aqueous preference operationally, but they cannot distinguish ordinary partitioning from ionization, association, or phase-specific handling effects.
- Most of the 4×4 catalyst–solvent matrix was untested, and extractants were not compared under a single replicated reaction and workup design.
- The effects of stirring speed, mixing time, settling time, catalyst loading, reaction concentration, phase ratio, and transfer fraction were largely untested because they were held fixed or absent during the campaign.

2. One additional discriminating experiment

I would run one C1/S2 reaction at 360 K for 7200 s, quench it, and split the well-mixed material into two equal aliquots. Each aliquot would receive identical aqueous and X3 volumes and identical mixing and settling. One aliquot would retain the aqueous phase and the other the organic phase. Both would be terminated with minimal additional processing and assayed. Measuring both retained phases from a common parent reaction would remove the independent-batch reaction variation that remains between batches 8 and 11.

My leading explanation predicts that most target recovery will appear in the aqueous aliquot, with the two phase recoveries approximately accounting for the parent target after allowing for sampling and handling losses. That result would substantially strengthen a genuine partition-based explanation.

If both aliquots had similar recovery, I would weaken the phase-preference claim and attribute much of the batch 8/11 difference to washing, drying, or independent process variation. If the organic aliquot had higher recovery, the current phase explanation would be rejected; batch 11’s poor result would then point primarily to its post-separation wash/dry sequence. If the summed recoveries were far below the pre-split target estimate despite small mass-balance error, I would consider quench chemistry, irreversible interfacial loss, or incompatibility between upstream and final-assay metrics rather than simple equilibrium partitioning.

3. Unused evidence, reliability, and goal effects

Evidence that received little or no mechanistic use included the raw synthetic spectra, peak assignments, and characterization artifacts; I relied on processed estimates. Degradation warnings were generally small and were not sufficient to fit degradation kinetics. Safety and cost observations were used only to confirm that safety did not bind; displayed cost saturated near 1 and was not informative for a quantitative model. Small final mass-balance errors supported internal consistency but did not identify where target was lost. The campaign also contained byproduct and impurity signals that were discussed qualitatively rather than fitted jointly. No independent replicate series was available for estimating process variance.

The sealed predictions are least reliable where they extrapolate furthest from campaign conditions. Q01–Q06 use a catalyst/reagent ratio one-twentieth of the campaign ratio, 400 K, different solvent and phase volumes, and an X2 organic endpoint that was never directly assayed. Their recovery predictions are therefore especially uncertain. Q07–Q12 restore the catalyst/reagent ratio but use only 0.002 mol reagent, much lower reaction concentration, 400 K, and new wash/transfer designs. The relative predictions for washing and wash staging are more defensible than their absolute values, but even those rest mainly on batches 11 and 12 and are confounded by extractant and reaction differences. The predicted X0-versus-X2 purity contrast and phase-ratio effects are particularly speculative. Q11 versus Q12 is also uncertain because the campaign did not isolate concentration as a paired factor.

The operating recommendation is likewise limited. Batch 8 was clearly the best observed recovery–purity compromise, but its purity was only 0.6189 and therefore failed the required 0.80 constraint. It should not be interpreted as a validated compliant process.

The assigned goal did affect evidence collection. Because the objective prioritized final recovery subject to purity, I spent all 12 nonfinal measurements on one HPLC observation per batch and all 12 final assays on completed processes. This provided broad recipe and workup comparisons but sacrificed time courses, true replication, direct assays of both phases, and systematic factor isolation. Later batches increasingly targeted the observed purification failure, which improved decision relevance but left the kinetic model sparse. I see no clear conflict between the goal and honest interpretation, but the optimization emphasis produced evidence better suited to selecting a best observed batch than to uniquely identifying mechanism.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 8 is the best completed batch observed: final assay recovery 0.2563 and purity 0.6189, both superior to the other meaningful-recovery products. It used the best-supported C1/S2 reaction recipe and retained the aqueous phase after X3 extraction. No batch met the required 0.80 purity, so this is explicitly a best-available recommendation rather than a constraint-satisfying process.
